title: The Furuta nineteen ninety eight paper

segs.text: Section twenty two. The Furuta nineteen ninety eight paper. H pylori is a bacterium that infects the stomach, and curing the infection treats diseases such as peptic ulcer. Furuta and colleagues treated sixty two Japanese patients with omeprazole, a proton pump inhibitor that lowers stomach acid, plus one antibiotic, amoxicillin. They compared cure rates by the patients' C Y P two C nineteen genotype. C Y P two C nineteen is the enzyme that clears omeprazole.

The patients were mostly middle aged men with a gastric or duodenal ulcer and H pylori infection. They took omeprazole twenty milligrams for eight weeks for a gastric ulcer or six weeks for a duodenal ulcer, plus amoxicillin five hundred milligrams four times a day for two weeks. That is one proton pump inhibitor with one antibiotic. In the United States, H pylori is usually treated with triple therapy, a proton pump inhibitor with two antibiotics.

The paper uses old names. It calls the enzyme S mephenytoin four prime hydroxylase. It calls the normal allele wild type, which is star one, and the two variants m one, which is star two, and m two, which is star three. Star two and star three are single base changes that create a premature stop codon, so the protein is too short to work. A person with any two of them has no active enzyme.

The patients fell into three groups. Group one had two normal copies, star one star one, so normal enzyme activity. Their cure rate was twenty eight point six percent, eight of twenty eight. Group two had one normal copy and one star two or star three, so some activity. Their cure rate was sixty percent, fifteen of twenty five. Group three had two inactive copies, so no activity. These are the poor metabolizers, and all nine were cured, one hundred percent. No patient was star three star three. Such a patient would simply belong in group three.

Less enzyme means more omeprazole stays in the body. Earlier work cited by the paper gave the relative omeprazole exposure in the three groups as one, three point seven and twenty. This paper did not measure omeprazole in the blood.

The paper gives four reasons why higher omeprazole levels improved cure. First, omeprazole stays high in poor metabolizers, so the stomach p H stays high for longer. Second, amoxicillin is unstable and less active at low p H, so a higher stomach p H leaves more active antibiotic.

Third, omeprazole raises the amount of amoxicillin in the gastric juice, where H pylori is, so the antibiotic stays in the stomach longer at levels that work. She said, something about omeprazole helps get the amoxicillin into the gastric juices and helps it stay intact there, cause you've increased the p H. Fourth, omeprazole has some activity against H pylori of its own, presumably greater in poor metabolizers.

Ulcer healing followed the cure rates. In group three every gastric and every duodenal ulcer healed, and the ulcer healed in every patient who was cured. The authors credit this to the higher cure rate and the stronger acid suppression in poor metabolizers.

Does the result apply in the United States? She said, Not on the face of it. The poor metabolizer genotype is eighteen to twenty three percent in Japanese persons but three to five percent in white U S or European populations, so the group sizes differ. With genotyping, the same response is expected for the same genotype, and fewer antibiotics might be enough for the right genotypes.
